profile.reading:
Digital Realty PDX11 is tagged in mapping data as a Digital Realty building at 6676 Northeast 62nd Avenue in Hillsboro, Oregon, part of the Washington County corridor that has become one of the most heavily built data center clusters in the United States. Digital Realty, a publicly traded data center real estate investment trust, is a long established presence in the area, but the company's own current Portland market overview page names only two active Hillsboro campuses by their public designations, PDX10 at 3825 Northwest Aloclek Street and PDX12 at 5870 Northeast Schaaf Street, describing roughly 594,000 combined square feet of colocation space with 2N+1 cooling redundancy and SOC 1, SOC 2, SOC 3, PCI-DSS, and ISO 27001 compliance. PDX11 does not appear as a separately named facility on that page as of this research, which is a genuine gap rather than an oversight to paper over. It may be that PDX11 is a support or shell building folded into the marketed campus description, that its public name has changed, or that the marketing page has simply not been kept current. None of the operator's own published material found for this project confirms an IT load, generator rating, or utility feed for a building specifically called PDX11 at this address, and none is invented here.

What is well documented is why any Digital Realty building in this stretch of Hillsboro exists at all. The corridor grew up around Intel's semiconductor campuses and kept growing because Oregon carries no state sales tax and because Washington County and the City of Hillsboro have run some of the country's most aggressive local property tax abatement programs, granted through Oregon's enterprise zone statute and, for the largest projects, the state's Strategic Investment Program. The City of Hillsboro's own accounting, current as of July 21, 2026, counted 23 data center sites within city limits, 16 already built across 346 acres and seven more in permitting or under construction across another 224 acres, together about 570 of the city's roughly 17,378 total acres. Property tax abatements tied to those data centers ran three to five years per project, covered about 7.2 billion dollars of otherwise taxable real market value out of roughly 11 billion dollars in assessed value in 2025, and still yielded about 61.1 million dollars in total taxes paid that year. Trade press has reported that Hillsboro's abatements saved data center operators and their customers 5.4 million dollars in 2018 and 3.1 million dollars in 2019, an earlier and smaller stage of the same policy. By law, Oregon shields the identity of individual enterprise zone applicants, so the city's own materials describe activity only in aggregate, most recently citing eight companies applying across eleven sites, without naming which companies or buildings.

Power access is the other half of the story. Portland General Electric, the utility serving Hillsboro, has said publicly that roughly 800 megawatts of data center load already operates in Hillsboro against a system wide load of about 4.5 gigawatts, with about 3 gigawatts of additional data center interconnection requests pending, and it has partnered with a startup called GridCARE on grid flexibility tools it says freed more than 80 megawatts of near term interconnection capacity and could allow over 400 more megawatts to energize by 2029. Those are utility wide figures describing the whole Hillsboro data center footprint, not a number attributable to this one building, and they are recorded here as regional context rather than as this facility's own utility power figure. Growth has also outpaced the city's zoning rules, on July 27, 2026 Hillsboro's City Council imposed a 120 day moratorium on new data center and battery storage land use applications and opened a two phase rewrite of its development code, with use and definition standards due in fall 2026 and design standards to follow in winter or spring 2027. Whether this specific building predates or falls under that moratorium's review is not stated in any source found, and is left unanswered rather than assumed.

reading.body:
This facility cannot be ranked among Oregon's published capacity because no IT load, utility feed, or generator rating for Digital Realty PDX11 appears in any operator or government source found. Digital Realty operates two named campuses in Hillsboro on different streets, PDX10 and PDX12, described together as roughly 594,000 square feet with SOC 1, SOC 2, SOC 3, PCI-DSS, and ISO 27001 compliance. PDX11 does not appear on Digital Realty's current Portland market page, which is a genuine gap rather than an oversight. The address here, 6676 Northeast 62nd Avenue, cannot be matched to a confirmed operator building this session, so no square footage or power draw is published.

Hillsboro itself is one of the most heavily built data center clusters in the United States, driven by Oregon's property tax abatement programs and proximity to Intel's semiconductor facilities. The city counted 23 data center sites within its limits as of July 2026, with 16 already built across 346 acres and seven more in permitting or construction. Oregon law shields individual enterprise zone applicant identities, so the identity of which operators or buildings receive abatements cannot be disclosed. On July 27, 2026, Hillsboro imposed a 120 day moratorium on new data center applications and opened a full rewrite of its development code, making the status of any new facility unclear.

Portland General Electric reported roughly 800 megawatts of data center load operating in Hillsboro against about 4.5 gigawatts of system wide load, with about 3 gigawatts of additional data center interconnection requests pending. The utility partnered with GridCARE on grid flexibility tools it says freed over 80 megawatts of near term capacity and could enable over 400 additional megawatts by 2029. These are utility wide figures for the whole Hillsboro corridor, not specific to this building, and they reflect that power access, not land or tax policy alone, is now the binding constraint on data center growth in the region.
